title: New Study Finds Creatine May Boost Strength After 45, Even Without Exercise
excerpt: A 12-week trial of 64 middle-aged adults found that creatine supplementation improved lean mass and muscle strength — with modest gains observed even among those who did not work out.
body:
• A 12-week study of 64 adults ages 45–65 found that creatine supplementation improved lean tissue mass, muscle strength, and markers of cognitive function — especially when combined with exercise.
  • Even participants who did not exercise showed slight improvements in lean mass, strength, and cognitive function after taking 10 grams of creatine daily.
  • Experts caution the trial was small and short, and creatine should not replace exercise — but say the findings support its potential as a tool for preserving muscle health with age.
  • Most adults can benefit from a standard daily dose of 3 to 5 grams of creatine monohydrate, which is generally well-tolerated.

Creatine, a supplement long associated with gym-goers and competitive athletes, may have broader benefits for people entering middle age — including those who don't exercise regularly, according to a new study published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition.

The 12-week trial recruited 64 adults between the ages of 45 and 65, assigning roughly half to take 10 daily grams of creatine monohydrate and the rest to receive a placebo. Within both groups, some participants also followed a structured diet and completed a three-day-per-week regimen of resistance exercise and cardio training.

Gains Across the Board

Among those who exercised, creatine produced clear advantages. Participants in the supplement group showed improved lean tissue mass, greater muscle strength, enhanced cognitive function markers, and a sharper reduction in body fat percentage compared with the placebo group.

The surprise was in the non-exercising cohort. Even without physical training, those taking creatine showed modest but measurable improvements in lean mass, strength, and selected cognitive markers.

"Of course, you get better effects with training. But the research suggests anybody can take creatine and get some benefit."

— Richard Kreider, PhD, FACSM, Texas A&M University

Kreider, who directs the Exercise & Sport Nutrition Lab at Texas A&M and co-authored the study, said the findings point to creatine as an accessible supplement that can support muscle health regardless of exercise habits.

Why It Matters for Aging Adults

The body naturally produces creatine, which helps generate adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — the energy currency that muscles use to contract during short bursts of intense activity. Supplementing creatine increases intramuscular phosphocreatine stores by roughly 20 to 40 percent, according to prior research.

This becomes especially relevant after 45, when age-related muscle loss — a condition known as sarcopenia — accelerates. Hormone changes, reduced protein intake, underlying medical conditions, and sedentary habits all contribute to declining muscle mass and strength. Muscles also become progressively less responsive to exercise over time.

Haris Vakil, a sports medicine physician at Houston Methodist Clear Lake Hospital who was not involved in the study, said the results "add to an already growing body of evidence supporting creatine as a potential tool for preserving muscle health as we age."

A Word of Caution

Despite the encouraging findings, experts urged restraint. The trial was small and relatively brief, and the lean mass gains observed in non-exercisers may partly reflect creatine's "cellular swelling" effect rather than actual muscle growth. Creatine draws water into muscle cells, which can increase measured mass without building new tissue.

Anthea Levi, a registered dietitian not involved in the study, cautioned against treating creatine as a substitute for physical activity. "Creatine can be a good option for people who exercise as a way to potentially get more out of the work they're already doing," she said.

A 2026 systematic review examining postmenopausal women specifically found that creatine produced small improvements in lean mass and strength when paired with resistance training, but did not significantly improve bone density.

Practical Guidance

For most adults, 3 to 5 grams of creatine monohydrate daily is the standard effective dose — the study used 10 grams, but experts say smaller amounts achieve similar results over a few weeks. Loading phases of 20-plus grams per day, popular among athletes, are generally unnecessary for everyday supplementation.

Creatine monohydrate remains the most studied and affordable form. More expensive variants have not been shown to be superior. The supplement is considered safe and well-tolerated for most people, though it can cause water retention and occasional gastrointestinal discomfort. People with kidney or liver disease should consult a healthcare provider before starting.

Consistency matters more than timing, Vakil said: "The best time to take creatine is the time you're most likely to remember to take it."
